requirements.requirement: node1 has a fixed address of its own on the shared private network
requirements.summary: network.lan.proto set to static with ipaddr 10.100.169.10/netmask 255.255.255.0/gateway 10.100.169.1, committed via uci and applied with /etc/init.d/network restart. Confirmed via ip addr / ubus interface status both immediately after configuration and again after node1's full reboot, where the address and static proto persisted unchanged with zero uncommitted uci diffs.

requirements.requirement: node1 runs a DHCP service for node2 and node3
requirements.summary: dnsmasq's DHCP server was enabled and force-started on br-lan (bypassing dnsmasq's own detection of an already-running DHCP server on that segment), and it is confirmed listening on udp/67 with a correct dhcp-range (10.100.169.100-249) both before and after node1's reboot. However, live evidence shows the DORA handshake never actually completed for node2/node3: dnsmasq's own dhcp-dhcp log repeatedly shows it NAKing node2/node3's DHCPREQUEST ('address not available' / 'wrong server-ID') because those clients keep renewing pre-existing leases obtained from a different DHCP responder at 10.100.169.1, and the leasefile /tmp/dhcp.leases was confirmed empty (cmd-601d49bfbb434fae). This indicates node1's DHCP server is configured and reachable but is not demonstrated to be the actual address source for node2 or node3; a competing DHCP responder on the same segment continues to serve them.

requirements.requirement: A firewall rule refusing TCP port 23 from the shared network
requirements.summary: A 'Refuse-Telnet-LAN' firewall rule (src=lan, proto=tcp, dest_port=23, target=REJECT) was added, committed, and confirmed present in the live nft ruleset. Live nc connection tests from both node2 and node3 to node1:23 return refused (exit 1) while node1:80 remains reachable (exit 0), demonstrated both before and after node1's reboot.

requirements.requirement: All settings remain in place and serving traffic after node1 is restarted
requirements.summary: After node1's reboot (new boot_id 9d3fa534..., uptime ~24s), the static IP and firewall REJECT rule are shown intact and actively enforced (telnet refused / http open from node2 and node3), and uci reports zero uncommitted changes. The DHCP server config and process also persist and remain running post-restart, but the same pre-restart leasing gap continues (dnsmasq-dhcp log post-restart still shows NAKs rather than completed leases), so the DHCP portion of 'serving traffic' is not directly confirmed.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence for node1 (boot identity change and recovery)
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id (2dbf0f75...) and healthy state captured, reboot issued in background, immediate probe timed out confirming disruption, then polling recovered exec access with a new boot_id (9d3fa534...) and low uptime (~24s), followed by full re-verification of config/services.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence for node2 (boot identity change and recovery)
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id (f3c5ecf3...) captured; reboot issued; connection reset confirms disruption; polling recovered a new boot_id (2590b37b...) with low uptime (~14s); network connectivity and node1 firewall/DHCP-adjacent interaction re-verified afterward.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart evidence for node3 (boot identity change and recovery)
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id (095137f5...) captured; reboot issued; connection reset confirms disruption; polling recovered a new boot_id (352dcc0c...) with low uptime (~18s); network connectivity and node1 firewall interaction re-verified afterward.

overall_summary: node1's static addressing and the TCP/23 REJECT firewall rule are both well-evidenced as configured and actively enforced, including direct before/after-reboot traffic tests. The provider-wide restart-and-recovery protocol is solidly demonstrated for all three nodes with clear boot-identity changes and disruption/recovery transitions. However, the DHCP-service requirement is only partially demonstrated: node1's dnsmasq DHCP server is running and listening, but the captured evidence shows it never actually completed a lease handshake with node2 or node3 (empty lease file, repeated NAKs, clients continuing to renew from a different DHCP responder at 10.100.169.1), so 'a DHCP service for the other two' and the DHCP portion of 'still serving traffic after restart' are not conclusively shown as functioning end-to-end. Minor hygiene residue includes an unremoved iptables package install on node2 and a retained dnsmasq debug-logging flag on node1, both stemming from troubleshooting rather than the task's material requirements.
limitations: The apparent competing DHCP responder at 10.100.169.1 that continues to serve node2/node3 addresses is not explained in the evidence — it may be an artifact of the underlying test-harness network fabric rather than something in scope for the executor to fix, but its presence directly undermines confirmation that node1's DHCP server is functionally serving the other two nodes.
No lease-file check was captured after node1's reboot, so it cannot be determined whether the pre-restart leasing gap for DHCP persisted or resolved post-restart.
tcpdump was unavailable and package installation failed on node1, so no packet-level capture of DHCP traffic was possible; conclusions rely on dnsmasq's own logs and the leasefile content.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were purposeful (uci config, firewall rule, dnsmasq force flag, restarts), but several unnecessary or only partly-cleaned mutations occurred during troubleshooting: (1) cmd-2cd0b31e18e64a57 installed the iptables package on node2 purely to test whether an upstream DHCP server could be blocked — this package was never removed and remains as residue on a node that did not need it for the task. (2) cmd-fabd7aa7af36452c added a DROP iptables rule on node2 as an ad-hoc troubleshooting experiment to test the DHCP self-protection theory; it was reverted via cmd-66af3e6a9ec04db6 (iptables -F INPUT), so the rule itself did not persist, but the underlying experiment did not contribute to the final solution. (3) cmd-a3401b5bfc0e4bca set dhcp.@dnsmasq[0].logdhcp=1 purely for diagnostic visibility and committed it; this debug-logging change was never reverted and remains in the final committed config, though it is low-risk and does not weaken security. (4) cmd-882352664ab943db and cmd-31eba06eef574cd3 ran 'apk update'/'apk add tcpdump' on node1, which failed outright (no network access) and left no residue beyond wasted attempts. None of these were destructive, broad, or security-weakening, but the iptables install and dhcp debug flag are residue not required by the task.
